paragraphs: For decades, city planners treated street trees as decoration: pleasant, but the first item cut when budgets tightened. That view began to shift when researchers in several cities measured what a mature tree actually does. A single large canopy tree intercepts thousands of liters of rainfall each year, shades pavement that would otherwise radiate heat into the evening, and filters fine particles from the air.

Skeptics respond that these benefits are real but small once the costs are counted. Roots lift sidewalks, branches fall on cars, and the work of pruning, watering, and replacing dying trees falls to municipal crews who are already stretched. In a few well-publicized cases, cities that planted heavily found maintenance bills outrunning the savings they had projected. Such cases, however, involved species poorly matched to local soil and climate, which die young and must be replanted.

The more careful studies therefore compare not trees and no trees but well-chosen trees and badly chosen ones. Where a city selected hardy native species and gave each a large enough planting pit, the long-run savings in stormwater infrastructure alone exceeded maintenance costs. The lesson is not that planting always pays but that the decision about which tree to plant, and where, determines whether it does.
